GDC Talk: Saving Game History or Dooming it to Oblivion

The talk was given by Jason Scott from the Internet Archive. Here are some excerpts:

The way that these things are destroyed are not really in these massive explosions... it tends to be apathy... that's where we lose history.

The thing about game and computer history is that it is both adored, and ignored. For many years it was just considered to be... just another product on the shelf. So we have a lot of software locked away in plastic, much of it destroyed, thrown away, or rotting away.

We're so lucky with computer history right now... If you go down to the Computer History Museum... there's Slug [Steven Russell], who programmed Computer Space. And he will play you. And he will kick your ass. And you will feel humbled. It's like a caveman showed up, and took you out. This is an amazing gift that we have, that our history is so [compact]. We lose people, but we still have so much access to it. But the other side to that, is that software half-life is ridiculous. ... Having a few months between the release of a game, and EA going, "What game?" is insane. ... The average multiplayer networked game is now nearing eighteen months of total life before they turn the servers off. So you have a year and a half to understand if it's even useful, and then it's gone.

Games are not just products, but they're [still] also products. ... Games are perceived as closed-off media things that should be protected intellectually, and then eventually will phase into the areas of history. ... ironically, they die with no trace almost immediately. ... a painting can sit unwanted for fifty years, and then somebody goes, "Oh wow, nobody knew that this painter made this." And suddenly people wanna know this story. ... Not so easy with games.

[Games] are building places and memories that will live with people for the rest of their lives. ... They're important. They will become part of the fabric of other peoples' lives.

This is a [forum] discussion of the saving of the Prince of Persia code... where we took stuff off of old floppy drives with Jordan Mechner. And Jordan was like, "What do I do with the source code now?" And I was like, "Put it on Github." And somebody came in, forked the [repository], and took away the copy protection. ... That is the ultimate sure-fire pirating technique. Game comes out, wait 33 years, it shows up on github, fork out all the protection, victory! But while this was all being discussed on MetaFilter, the original creator of the copy protection put up his original floppy up against the screen and took a picture. So once again, we're still in that world.

MAME ... is an easy [emulator] to poke fun at or go after. You're like, "Oh great, PAC-MAN lives forever." But it also goes after games for which the only evidence it ever existed is a single circuit board. ... They also did something called the MESS system, which goes after computer platforms. ... I was part of a group called Javascript MESS, and what we did was we ported MESS to Javascript. So, at the [Internet] Archive, you can click on many pieces of software from the'80s, and have it boot up in your browser in Javascript at full speed. ... I've been sent pictures from teachers who connect to Oregon Trail through us.

DOOM is the perfect storm. ... They saved their information, they took video tape of stuff they were working on, John Romero still has the boombox that was playing and he knows what tapes were playing when they were developing it.

Infocom. Beautiful place. They made text adventures for about 95% of you in the audience. And Steve Meretsky saved all the memos, all of the design documents and all the materials. ... If there's one thing that you need to learn from this whole thing, it is STEAL FROM WORK. ... If stuff lying around is gonna be thrown out, stick it in a box with the name of your company. You would be surprised what was able to be pulled from these. ... [Infocom] had to redesign their phone system and in doing so they gave a list of everyone who worked at the company, and what their title was at that exact moment in time. ... people writing books [on Infocom] were able to track down people, and their stories were heard.

Blood. It painted the walls of the bedroom. I looked around at the aftermath. The scene of the event that would destroy everything I had ever known.

We had all grown up in a world reading books and watching movies about monsters. We dreamed about how glorious it would be to slay vampires, or decapitate zombies. Killing monsters was nothing like they made it out to be.

My eyes shot open at seven thirty in the morning. A blood curdling scream echoed through the house. What’s happening? I reached into the night stand and pulled out a 9mm. Was there an intruder? The screams started again. They came from my daughters room at the end of the hall. My heart leapt into my throat, my arms and legs felt like they were made of lead. I pushed the fear aside, and dove for the door. The rhythmic beating of my heart matched my pace as I tore down the hallway.

As I neared her room everything fell suddenly silent. I burst into her bedroom door, shoulder first, ripping it from the hinges. My eyes caught sight of something. The adrenaline abandoned me and I was made of lead once more.

On the floor was my wife’s body, or what was left of it at least. Her face looked as though it had been eaten off by a pack of rabid dogs. Her blood was smeared across the walls like someone had been finger painting with it, her intestines sprinkled the floor like confetti.

My mouth tasted metallic as I fought back the urge to vomit. Tears blurred my vision. What kind of sick monster could do this? I had to look the bastard in the eyes before I slowly, painfully ended his life.

I raised my gaze. There it was tearing away chunks of flesh with its hands and mouth. It wasn’t a man, or a pack of rabid dogs. No. I couldn’t get that lucky. My three year old daughter crouched over her mother’s remains. Blood up to her elbows, and smeared across her mouth like barbecue sauce.

She stopped mid meal and glared at me with cold, dead eyes. Her head gave a sort of twitching jerk as she began gnashing her teeth. Bits of my wife falling out of her mouth.

She lunged at me. I raised my pistol. As tears clouded my vision once more I whispered, “Daddy loves you…” and squeezed the trigger. Her tiny body crumpled to the floor as the bullet pierced her skull. I fell with her, convulsing and sobbing.

I didn’t do it because I knew what she was. I did it, because the moment I saw her eyes I knew my sweet, little Tabby was dead. I knew it wasn’t her. The movies never told us about this. They never showed the hero sobbing and vomiting after shooting his own child. The movies lied.
